June 15, 2026 
Sc no.- 18932 
 
Dear Sir/Madam, 
 
 
 
Sub: Integrated Annual Report for the Financial Year 2025-26 and Notice convening the 
81st Annual General Meeting (‘AGM’) of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited 
(formerly Tata Motors Limited) (‘the Company’) 
 
 
This is in further reference to our letters dated May 14, 2026 and May 28, 2026, wherein we had 
informed that the 81st AGM of the Company will be held on Wednesday, July 8, 2026 at  
10:30 a.m. (IST) via Video Conference/Other Audio-Visual Means. 
 
Pursuant to Regulations 34(1) and 53(2) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (‘SEBI Listing Regulations’), we are enclosing herewith the 
Integrated Annual Report of the Company  including the Notice convening the 81st AGM and other 
Statutory Reports for the Financial Year 2025-26. The same is being sent through electronic mode 
to those Members/ Debenture Holders whose e-mail addresses are registered with the Company/ 
Registrar & Share Transfer Agent (‘RTA’)/ Depository Participant(s) (‘DPs’). Further, in 
accordance with the Regulations 36(1)(b) and 58(1)(b) of the SEBI Listing Regulations, the 
Company has initiated sending a letter, providing the web-link, including the exact path where 
complete details of the Integrated Annual Report including the Notice of AGM is available, to the 
shareholder(s) and debenture holder(s) who have not registered their e-mail addresses with the 
Company/RTA/DPs. 
 
The Integrated Annual Report including the Notice of the AGM is also available on the website of 
the Company at https://cars.tatamotors.com/investors/financial-information/annual-reports.html. 
 
This is for information of the Exchanges and the Members. 
 
Yours faithfully, 
Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited 
(formerly Tata Motors Limited) 
 
 
Maloy Kumar Gupta 
Company Secretary & Chief Legal Officer

Driven by Purpose

Our Founder
03.03.1839 – 19.05.1904
Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata

In a free enterprise, the 
community is not just another 
stakeholder in business, but 
is in fact the very purpose of 
its existence.

Mobility today is no longer just about getting from one place 
to another — it is about what that journey represents. It is 
an expression of aspiration, identity and responsibility. As 
customers seek smarter, safer and more sustainable ways 
to move, the role of mobility is being redefined — from a 
functional need to a purposeful choice.
At Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, we are responding 
to this shift with intention and clarity. We are not just 
building cars; we are shaping experiences that align with 
the evolving values of our customers — where design 
inspires, technology empowers, and sustainability is integral, 
not optional.
India stands at the forefront of this transformation 
— a market where design sensibilities are maturing, 
electric mobility is gaining momentum, and customer 
expectations are rising rapidly. In this dynamic landscape, 
our commitment is anchored in purpose: to create mobility 
solutions that are intuitive, future-ready and deeply relevant 
to the lives they serve.
Driven by Purpose reflects how we approach every 
dimension of our business. From reimagining product design, 
to advancing electrification through a robust EV portfolio, to 
embedding connected technologies that elevate safety and 
convenience — every decision is guided by a larger intent: to 
deliver meaningful value to our customers and stakeholders.
Our purpose extends beyond products. It shapes how we 
engage with our customers, strengthen our dealer and 
partner ecosystem, build capabilities within our workforce, 
and contribute meaningfully to the communities we serve. 
It guides us to create deeper, more intuitive connections 
— moving from transactions to relationships built on trust, 
transparency and delight. 
Within our organisation, it inspires a culture of continuous 
learning, innovation and accountability — equipping our 
people with the skills and mindset needed to lead in a 
rapidly evolving mobility landscape. Beyond business, 
it strengthens our commitment to responsible growth 
— advancing sustainable practices, fostering inclusivity 
and creating a positive social impact in every community 
we touch.
In essence, our purpose is not an abstract ideal — it is a 
lived commitment that informs every interaction, every 
decision and every action across our value chain. It drives 
us to empower our stakeholders as long-term collaborators 
in our growth journey, ensuring shared value and resilience 
across the ecosystem, driving us to adopt more sustainable 
practices across our operations and to contribute 
meaningfully to a cleaner, greener future.
As we move forward, this purpose will continue to define 
our path — enabling us to innovate with conviction, grow 
with responsibility, and create experiences that resonate far 
beyond the drive.
Because at Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, we are not just 
moving forward — we are Driven by Purpose.

Our key presence

Dear Shareholders,
It is my privilege to present the 81st Annual Report of Tata 
Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited (formerly Tata Motors 
Limited) for the financial year ended March 31, 2026—our 
first year as an exclusive, personal mobility company. 
This milestone follows the successful demerger and 
independent public listing of the Commercial Vehicles 
business and the renaming of your Company as Tata Motors 
Passenger Vehicles Limited, signalling our ambition to build 
a unique personal mobility franchise that strengthens 
its leadership in India’s passenger vehicles market and 
continues to create an exciting global presence in the 
modern luxury space through JLR. I would like to thank all 
colleagues, who contributed with commitment and rigor  
to the successful execution of the demerger.
The year 2026 began with expectations of steady global 
growth, soft inflation and easier financial conditions. 
However, the introduction of US tariffs in May 2025 created 
significant challenges globally. India responded by reducing 
its GST rates to boost domestic consumption which helped 
prop up domestic growth rates in the second half of the 
year. The year also witnessed positive developments 
including the signing of the landmark India-EU and India-UK 
Chairman’s message 
trade agreement, US-UK and the interim India-US trade deal. 
However, by early March, the start of the West Asia crisis 
brought rising concerns about stagflation—falling output 
coupled with rising inflation.
India
In India, your Company delivered strong operating and 
financial performance in fiscal 2026.
We delivered highest-ever sales of ~6.42 lakh cars and SUVs 
during the year, achieving robust year on year growth of 
15.3%, nearly twice the industry average. In the second 
half of the fiscal year, your Company emerged as the 
second largest player in the industry, with a market share 
of 14.1%, reflecting the growing scale, competitiveness and 
effectiveness of our multi-powertrain strategy.
Growth during the year was broad based, marked by a clear 
shift in customer preference and sales momentum towards 
greener powertrains. The strength and relevance of our 
product portfolio were clearly demonstrated through the 
following achievements:
•	 Nexon and Punch emerging as the #1 and #3 highest 
selling models in the industry in second half of the fiscal 
year, reflecting growing customer preference. 
N Chandrasekaran
Chairman

We enter FY27 with confidence, supported by a 
robust pipeline of new launches and multi-powertrain 
offerings. Our focus will remain on delivering industry-
leading growth, deepening our commitment to 
safety, sustainability, quality and customer delight, 
while becoming resilient and staying agile amid 
macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainties.
•	 Successful launch of the new Sierra by reviving a true 
icon of the Indian automotive landscape to widespread 
acclaim and registering a strong market response with 
record customer bookings. 
•	 Sales of CNG-powered vehicles outpacing industry 
growth, underscoring our ability to anticipate and 
respond to evolving customer preferences. 
•	 Re-entry in the South African market marked a strategic 
step forward towards greater internationalisation.
Your Company remains a clear market leader in Electric 
Vehicles, surpassing the cumulative milestone of 250,000 
EVs and commanding a dominant two thirds share of all EVs 
sold in India till date. In the fiscal 2026, your Company sold 
over 92,000 EVs marking a 43.4% growth over the previous 
year. The Company has been the #1 player in the market 
consistently for over the past 7 years with the current 
market share being 40.2%. 
Over the past few years, your Company has delivered 
sustained value creation- achieving growth at a CAGR of 
approximately 30%, with volumes expanding nearly five fold 
and revenues increasing close to six fold, while significantly 
enhancing customer access and convenience by doubling its 
sales and service network across the country. 
Your Company’s CSR initiatives continued to create 
meaningful impact through integrated village development, 
water stewardship and community resilience programmes, 
supported by sustained investments in skills, education 
and healthcare. During the year, our social interventions 
benefited over 18 lakh citizens across 105 districts, with 
over 52% of beneficiaries from marginalized communities, 
reinforcing our commitment to inclusive development. Key 
initiatives included the rejuvenation of over 1,000 water 
bodies across 20 districts in Maharashtra benefitting more 
than 6 lakh people, education programmes impacting 
over 2 lakh students, and targeted efforts enabling worthy 
aspirants to secure admissions to leading engineering and 
medical institutions.
The business delivered revenues of ₹58,465 crore, 
registering a healthy growth of 20.7% over FY25 with steady 
EBITDA and EBIT margins of 6.9% and 1.4% respectively. The 
PBT (bei) for the year stood at ₹1,436 crore, a 32.6% increase 
over FY25. The balance sheet remained robust with net cash 
position of ₹6,710 crore, underscoring the commitment 
to financial discipline while continuing to step-up on 
investments to deliver industry beating growth.

CHAIRMAN’S MESSAGE
Jaguar Land Rover: Resilience  
through a period of change
FY26 was a challenging year for Jaguar Land Rover, shaped 
by a confluence of internal and external disruptions. JLR 
was impacted by the introduction of incremental US tariffs 
impacting the exports from the UK to EU and the US. 
Additionally, the cyber incident resulted in your Company 
having to pause production for five weeks. These challenges 
reinforce the importance of resilience across strategy, 
vehicle architecture and powertrain choices, while needing 
to remain committed to technology investment. 
Revenues for the year were GBP 22,911 million down by 
20.9% compared to the previous year with results impacted 
by production pause due to the cyber incident. 
The year also marked a leadership transition with the 
retirement of Adrian Mardell, who dedicated 35 years to JLR 
and led the Company through an enormous transformation. 
With the appointment of PB Balaji as the CEO, JLR will 
continue to build on strong foundations as it enters its next 
phase of growth.
Consolidated Financials: On a consolidated basis, the business 
delivered revenues of ₹335,582 crore and PBT (bei) of ₹2,519 
crore for the year. The consolidated financial metrics for the 
year were impacted due multiple headwinds at JLR, including 
the production pause for five weeks due to the cyber incident. 
However, with return to normalcy of production and the 
continued demand momentum in the India PV business, the 
Company delivered a strong quarter in Q4FY26 with revenues 
of ₹105,447 crore and PBT (bei) of ₹7,167 crore.    
The Board of Directors have recommended a final dividend of 
₹3/- per share for Fiscal 26, subject to your approval.
Trends shaping mobility 
Rapid global advances in digital technologies and AI 
are transforming how mobility products are designed, 
experienced and supported. At the same time, the transition 
to clean energy, heightened expectations on safety, and 
the reconfiguration of global supply chains are redefining 
competitiveness. Geopolitical and uneven economic 
recovery are adding further complexity, making agility and 
resilience critical capabilities. 
India’s mobility transition is being shaped by—aspiration, 
infrastructure and evolving consumer expectations. The 
sustained demand supports the ICE portfolio and the 
continued momentum in EVs reflects growing customer 
confidence in new technologies underscoring the strength of 
a balanced, multi powertrain strategy of your Company. 
Looking ahead
We enter FY27 with confidence, supported by a robust 
pipeline of new launches and multi-powertrain offerings. 
Our focus will remain on delivering industry-leading growth, 
deepening our commitment to safety, sustainability, quality 
and customer delight, while becoming resilient and staying 
agile amid macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainties. 
Your Company will continue to focus on building 
distinctive, trusted and aspirational brands that connect 
meaningfully with customers. For Jaguar Land Rover, this is 
embodied in its House of Brands strategy, creating sharply 
differentiated luxury brands with clear identities, purpose 
and desirability. JLR will additionally focus on reducing 
its breakeven levels which has been impacted by tariffs, 
currency and commodities inflation, back to 300K units 
in the next 2 years whilst remaining focused on delivering 
exceptional launches of its New Range Rover Electric, 
Jaguar Type 01 and continue to build its Modern Luxury 
franchise. At Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, this thinking 
is reflected in the introduction of a more purposeful brand 
proposition, sharpening our focus on aspiration, trust and 
customer centricity. 
Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles and Jaguar Land Rover will 
continue to collaborate on manufacturing, technology and 
people, enhancing scale efficiencies, accelerating learning and 
reinforcing capital discipline. Early progress is evident with the 
commencement of operations at the new Panapakkam facility 
in Tamil Nadu, creating a shared manufacturing facility for 
best practice execution and scale benefits. 
Your Company will continue to embed digital technologies and 
AI across the value chain, build strong advanced analytics and 
leverage connected technologies to deliver personalised and 
proactive customer engagement. 
Guided by Project Aalingana, the Tata Group’s vision for a 
greener, cleaner and more equitable future, sustainability 
remains integral to your Company. With electrification at the 
core of substantiality, we are committed to being Net Zero 
by 2040. Your Company will continue to invest in products, 
platforms and ecosystems for accessible and scalable zero 
emission mobility solutions, while continuing to improve 
conventional powertrains.
On behalf of the Board, I would like to thank the employees, 
customers, suppliers and shareholders, for your continued 
trust and support. We are committed to moving forward with 
confidence in our strategy, optimism about our opportunities, 
and a strong focus on creating long-term value.
Warm Regards,
N Chandrasekaran

Operating environment 
The automotive industry is operating in a dynamic and complex environment 
shaped by evolving consumer preferences, heightened competition, shortening 
product cycles, regulatory shifts and policy divergence, cost pressures and 
geopolitical uncertainties. 
These factors have added layers of complexity and growth opportunities, which 
players will need to navigate with increasing agility and strategic clarity to win. 
Resilient  
business strategy
In today’s world, automotive OEMs are increasingly 
adopting resilient, flexible business strategies anchored 
around portfolio diversification, multi powertrain 
offerings, and agile operating models to succeed across 
markets. A balanced portfolio approach covering 
future-ready powertrains is becoming increasingly 
more important to address a wider spectrum 
of customer needs. At the same time, strategic 
localisation, supplier diversification and proactive risk 
management are becoming critical to strengthening 
supply chain resilience. Simultaneously, disciplined 
cost management, value engineering and scalable 
platforms are emerging as key imperatives to enable 
manufacturers to strengthen margins and remain 
competitive despite uncertainties. 
Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited is strengthening 
resilience through a diversified product portfolio, multi 
powertrain strategy, localised and agile operating 
models, and disciplined cost and risk management to 
navigate uncertainties while supporting sustainable 
growth. In FY26, in a tough competitive environment, 
the domestic business delivered highest ever volumes 
and became #2 player in H2 through multiple product 
interventions and agile actions to manage demand post 
GST 2.0 rollout. JLR is evolving its operating model to 
further centre around its House of Brands, growing 
each brand’s distinct identity and value to increase 
desirability and emotional connection with its clients. 
JLR has deployed a flexible powertrain approach 
to manage the slower-than-expected transition to 
electrification, offering a mix of ICE, PHEV and soon to 
be BEV powertrain options on its MLA platform.

Advancing electric mobility
Our EV journey marked a defining step this year as we crossed 
2.5 lakh cumulative sales. Through the year, our decisive 
focus was towards mainstreaming EVs by systematically and 
holistically addressing the barriers to their adoption.
We did this by re-engineering the value proposition of 
our EVs, bringing their acquisition costs closer to their ICE 
equivalents, enhancing range, improving charging speeds, and 
strengthening ownership confidence through initiatives such 
as lifetime battery warranty. Launches like Harrier.ev and New 
Punch.ev reflect this approach, combining aspiration with 
practicality to appeal to a wider set of customers.
In parallel, we scaled the charging ecosystem, expanding 
charging access through partnerships with charge point 
operators and our own Tata.ev Mega Charging Hubs, while 
improving reliability through verified charging solutions.
This integrated push across product and ecosystem drove 
over 43% year-on-year growth, with EV volumes exceeding 
92,000 units, as we sustained clear market leadership with  
a 40.2% share.
Customer experience and brand trust
Enhancing customer experience and delivering sustained 
customer delight remains a core priority for our business. 
To that end, our sales outreach was broadened significantly 
this year, with over 100 new outlets added to reach a wider 
set of buyers across geographies. We also accelerated 
the expansion of our service footprint, adding 1,600 new 
workshop bays and strengthening existing facilities with 
digitised diagnostic and technical support capabilities. 
Collectively, these initiatives improved responsiveness 
across touchpoints, strengthened product quality, and 
elevated the overall ownership experience, reflected in  
a rise in our Net Promoter Score to 52.
Manufacturing and supply chain readiness
Aligned with growing demand for our products, we made 
significant progress in strengthening and modernising our 
manufacturing footprint. Alongside capacity augmentation 
and increased digitisation across existing plants, we 
commenced operations at our new joint manufacturing 
facility with Jaguar Land Rover in Tamil Nadu, enhancing 
our readiness for future growth. We also deepened the 
deployment of artificial intelligence across our operations, 
leveraging it to drive improvements in product quality, 
enhance manufacturing efficiency, and strengthen workforce 
safety. In parallel, we continued to build increasingly localised, 
agile, high quality, and robust supply chains to support scale 
and resilience as we navigate a complex geopolitical climate.
Embedding sustainability
Sustainability continues to be embedded deeply across 
our operations and decision making as we advance toward 
our goal of achieving Net Zero emissions by 2040. During 
the year, we reduced our carbon footprint across the 
value chain through higher adoption of renewable energy, 
increased penetration of greener powertrains, and cross-
deployment of best practices. We also progressed on 
broader environmental priorities, including circularity 
and biodiversity, with clear pathways and governance 
frameworks now in place.
Advancing community wellbeing
Our commitment to social responsibility remained steadfast 
through the year, with CSR programmes delivering tangible 
outcomes across our operating regions. We continued 
to invest in water stewardship and the rejuvenation of 
community water bodies, strengthening both livelihoods and 
environmental sustainability. Alongside, our focus on skill 
development, education, and healthcare access helped drive 
meaningful change in the communities around us, further 
amplified by active employee volunteering participation. These 
efforts reinforce our conviction that building a responsible and 
sustainable business goes well beyond the factory floor.
Looking ahead
While the industry will need to closely monitor ongoing 
geopolitical developments, the fundamental demand 
drivers of the Indian passenger vehicles market remain 
strong, with growth expected to be led by SUV, CNG, and 
EV segments. We enter FY27 with confidence, supported by 
stronger fundamentals, a robust pipeline of new launches, 
multi powertrain offerings, and renewed momentum 
from the second half of FY26. Our focus will remain on 
delivering industry leading growth while deepening our 
commitment to safety, sustainability, quality, and customer 
delight. At the same time, we will continue to ensure 
agility and resilience in our execution as we navigate the 
geopolitical environment. 
I remain confident that your Company is well positioned to 
create long term value for all stakeholders. This confidence 
is founded on the passion, resilience and talent of our 
people, and the enduring trust that our customers and you, 
our shareholders, place in us. Thank you for your continued 
support and belief in our journey.
Warm regards,

Robust industry growth in H2 post GST 2.0
After a slow start in H1, where growth rates were flat, the 
PV industry saw a sharp rebound in demand post GST 2.0 in 
September 2025. Reduced GST rates resulted in improved 
affordability which helped drive demand across segments, 
resulting in strong double-digit growth in H2 FY26. As a 
result, the industry saw record annual volumes of over 
4.7 million units for FY26, and will head into FY27 with 
significant demand momentum. 
Key transitions in bodystyle and 
technology preferences 
Post GST 2.0, industry growth has been disproportionately 
strong in Sub Compact, Compact, and Mid SUVs, 
reinforcing India’s sustained preference for the SUV 
bodystyle. Additionally, there was strong growth in 
greener powertrains, i.e. CNG vehicles & EVs, reflecting 
growing customer preference. Simultaneously, customer 
expectations for in vehicle technology have risen sharply 
across segments. Entry categories increasingly demand 
richer feature sets, while higher segments are adopting 
advanced systems including ADAS suites, auto park assist 
etc., which are setting new benchmarks in premium mobility. 
Safety has also become a decisive purchase criterion, with 
rising consumer preference for 5 star rated vehicles and 
models equipped with comprehensive active and passive 
safety systems.
EV momentum strengthens on OEM 
participation and ecosystem maturity 
EV adoption accelerated in FY26, supported by the 
continued 5% GST for EVs and strong OEM participation. 
New high aspiration EV launches expanded category 
consideration, while coordinated marketing efforts by 
OEMs helped build awareness and reinforce customer 
confidence. At the same time, charging infrastructure 
surpassed over 30,000 public charging stations improving in 
reliability, highway coverability, and residential accessibility, 
making ownership more seamless. These developments 
collectively strengthened EV momentum and positioned EVs 
as an expanding and structurally important part of India’s 
powertrain landscape.

Geopolitics 
Evolving regulatory frameworks, including use of further 
tariff and non-tariff protectionism mechanisms as well 
as conflicts, such as that in the Middle East would have a 
material adverse effect on our business prospects, results 
and financial condition. The secondary consequences 
of such geopolitical events may include further financial 
instability and slower economic growth in the UK, 
continental Europe and globally. They could also impact 
our supply chains or otherwise constrain our ability to 
operate efficiently.
Despite having manufacturing sites around the world, our 
primary activities are in the UK and Europe and are vulnerable 
to changes in trade tariffs. Although smaller in terms of 
overall volume, our other manufacturing facilities located 
around the rest of the world, including China, India and Brazil, 
could also be vulnerable to shifts in global trade and economic 
policies, and the fallout from the conflict in the Middle East.. 
Any adverse changes to tariff policies on a global basis could 
have a material adverse effect on our business prospects, 
results of operations and financial condition. 
During 2025, we experienced the effect of this through 
incremental US tariffs applied to our exports from the UK 
and EU. Subsequent trade deals between the UK and US and 
the EU and US as well as the relaxation of the US emission 
regulations have reduced the impact on the business, but 
they continue to add to the cost and uncertainty of doing 
business in the US.
Demand and competition
Consumer demand continues to be affected by uncertainty 
surrounding electric vehicles, particularly concerns related 
to range, the availability of charging infrastructure and lower 
residual values. High upfront costs for vehicle purchases 
and home charging installation, combined with fluctuating 
government incentives, further contribute to hesitation and 
delays among potential buyers.
In addition, market conditions are becoming more 
challenging because of increased competition, especially 
from Chinese manufacturers in UK and European markets. 
The introduction of the China Luxury Tax has added 
further pressure in the local China market, making higher 
value vehicles even more expensive for consumers or 
adding pressure on margins for OEMs through additional 
discounting in China and other regions where they try to 
reallocate production.
Supply chain risks 
The automotive requirement for rare earth elements and 
other specialised materials in electric vehicle production 
presents a significant critical-mineral supply risk. 
Additionally, natural disasters and human driven events, 
such as labour disputes, have the potential to disrupt the 
just-in-time manufacturing process, creating further supply 
chain vulnerabilities.
Cyber 
Cybersecurity risks remain elevated, as malicious actors 
continue to target all types of organisations and cause 
disruption, as we experienced in 2025. As products and 
services across all industries become more technologically 
advanced and connected, cybersecurity considerations 
remain an evolving area of focus for businesses. These global 
cybersecurity risks range from isolated, uncoordinated 
attempts to highly sophisticated and targeted attacks, 
referred to as advanced persistent threats.

determine which sustainability issues are most important to 
the organisation and its stakeholders. It involves evaluating 
the organisation’s impact on environmental and social 
factors (inside-out perspective) and examining how these 
factors affect the organisation (outside-in perspective). This 
dual approach helps the Company identify and prioritise 
ESG issues that are both financially important and socially 
significant, promoting the comprehensive integration of 
sustainability into its core strategy. We plan to conduct 
similar assessments every two years, taking emerging 
sustainability issues, global events and other trends

efficiency, enabling effective decision making

security requirements.

disruption to business-critical operations,

Life Cycle Assessments (LCAs)
In line with its commitment to Sustainability, we conduct 
comprehensive Life Cycle Assessments (LCAs) to evaluate the 
environmental impacts of its products. These assessments 
examine resource use, ecological impacts such as greenhouse 
gas (GHG) emissions and ecotoxicity, as well as human 
health considerations including human toxicity and ionising 
radiation. LCAs quantify these impacts using established 
indicators such as Global Warming Potential, Acidification 
Potential, Eutrophication Potential, Abiotic Depletion, Ozone 
Layer Depletion, and Photochemical Ozone Creation Potential.
Cradle-to-Grave LCA has been completed for the Nexon 
ICE and EV variants, with third-party validation. In addition, 
Cradle-to-Gate internal LCA assessments have been conducted 
for multiple passenger vehicle models, including Tiago, Tigor, 
Punch, Nexon, Curvv, Harrier MCE, Safari MCE, Sierra, Tiago EV, 
Tigor EV, Nexon EV, Punch EV, Curvv EV, and Harrier EV.
To better understand the lifecycle impacts of EV battery 
cells, a Cradle-to-Gate analysis was also conducted with the 
support of a third-party consultant. This study evaluates 
the global supply-chain impacts of battery manufacturing, 
including the influence of different manufacturing locations, 
such as China and India.
These LCA studies help in identification of ‘hotspots’ where 
environmental impacts are most significant, enabling 
targeted improvements to reduce product carbon footprint, 
minimise waste generation and promote use of sustainable 
materials. We have systematically embedded these 
objectives in our product development process by setting 
decarbonisation and material circularity targets for future 
passenger vehicle models.
Nexon ICE & EV - An LCA landmark:
Building on the earlier Cradle-to-Grave Life Cycle Assessment 
of the Tata Nexon Diesel variant, the Company has now 
completed a comprehensive and independently verified LCA 
for the Nexon EV across different battery capacities, setting  
a new benchmark in its sustainability practices.
The study, conducted in accordance with ISO 14040 and 
ISO 14044 standards, evaluates environmental impacts 
across the vehicle’s entire lifecycle, covering all stages 
from raw material extraction through manufacturing 
and use to end-of-life treatment. This comprehensive 
environmental impact assessment is based on vehicle-level 
part material distribution, detailed mapping of all part 
manufacturing processes, and evaluation of upstream and 
downstream logistics. It also incorporates plant-level vehicle 
manufacturing emissions, well-to-tank and tank-to-wheel 
emissions, and end-of-life impacts derived from emission 
and resource consumption data from Registered Vehicle 
Scrapping Facilities (RVSFs).
The study has been independently verified by M/s TÜV 
Rheinland, enhancing the robustness and credibility of 
the methodology, results, and conclusions. The system 
boundary considered in the baseline study is illustrated in

3 	Preserving nature and biodiversity
Our biodiversity strategy is aligned with the Group’s 
Aalingana strategy, metrics and milestones, and puts in 
place an Action Plan for delivering a Net Positive Impact on 
biodiversity. At an enterprise level, the strategy lays down 
the steps to restore, enhance, and protect nature, ensuring  
a net positive outcome on biodiversity.
Our understanding of biodiversity and species extinction 
began with the senior leadership engaging with leading 
Subject Matter Experts and conservation practitioners, 
which helped to adopt a science-based approach as 
opposed to the ad-hoc actions. Strategic coherence led to 
the identification of 3 areas for biodiversity interventions 
which span (1) its own Operations, (2) its Value Chain and (3) 
beyond the Value Chain extending to the national landscape 
and aligning with national conservation priorities. For 
each of these areas, we adopted scientific frameworks and 
concepts, built ambition in line with our aspiration to move 
the needle and established baselines.
Through FY25 to FY26, we launched projects across all 
3 areas, which have strategic relevance and potential to 
deliver impact at scale. The projects are conceptualised 
to deliver scientifically validated approaches (as SOP’s) 
ready for implementation; for example eco-restoration of 
disturbed habitats or improving the health of threatened 
wetlands. Such initiatives, which leverage nature and 
productive ecosystems to protect people and biodiversity, 
constitute what are called Nature based Solution (NbS) 
projects. In the scale-up phase of this unique strategic 
approach, we plan to engage Value Chain partners and 
corporate peers, to adopt and implement these SOPs in 
similar landscapes, while continuing to provide stewardship, 
enable convergence funding and monitor impact. This 
strategy will realise ours and the Groups objective of 
investing in NbS projects in India to deliver biodiversity and 
community co-benefits.
3.1 Own operations
Since inception, all our Operational sites in India 
have demarcated dedicated areas on which green-belt and 
wetlands are developed. A comprehensive biodiversity 
baseline survey across all our plants was carried out to get an 
in-depth understanding of floristic and faunal diversity, extent 
of threats, presence of species with special conservation value 
and other challenges. This was followed by LiDAR based drone 
survey to map habitats, contours, surface water flow and 
other geographic features required for ecosystem restoration 
planning.  In FY26, a comprehensive eco-restoration master 
plan supported by scientific metrics is being developed 
for execution in next FY. The eco-restoration projects are 
structured to meet the criteria laid down in the MoEFCC-NBA-
UNDP backed OECM framework (i.e. Other Effective Area 
Based Conservation Measures) – which expands the scope 
of area-based conservation beyond legally protected areas. 
Going beyond certification, these Tata Motors Passenger 
Vehicles Limited ‘nature hot-spots’ set in the midst of 
industrial estates, will serve as a lighthouse of best practice 
in biodiversity conservation. We are engaging our employees 
and local stakeholders enabling awareness-building, research, 
and adoption to create a ripple effect far beyond its premises. 
At our recently inaugurated Panapakkam facility, a one-year 
seasonal baseline biodiversity assessment was conducted for 
integrating biodiversity conservation elements into operations 
and campus management. 
3.2 Value chain
Automobile manufacturing sources a diverse range of parts, 
materials and consumables from a complex global supply 
chain. This sourcing determines the level of both dependency 
and impact on nature and natural resources. To address 
this, we have been working on the corporate engagement 
programme of Science-Based Targets for Nature. This 
structured approach will help us reduce our contribution to 
key drivers of nature loss. In FY26, we have identified material 
impacts of our operations and those of our immediate 
upstream value chain on nature and biodiversity.
3.3 Beyond value chain
We are demonstrating leadership by addressing Nature 
and Biodiversity beyond its Operations and Value Chain 
in line with our ambition to create impact at scale. After 
evaluating a wide range of potential topics, we shortlisted 
3 projects aligned with the Kunming Montreal-Global 
Biodiversity Framework.
1.	
Wetlands & Winged Voyagers – Wetlands along the 
path of the Central Asian Flyway in India, are critical 
wintering habitats for millions of migratory birds, 
providing food and safe resting areas. Securing these 
wetlands is essential for the continuance of the annual 
global migration and avian biodiversity.
	
We are collaborating with Wetland International 
South Asia is heading the Wetland & Winged Voyagers 
project with the ambition of creating wetland-positive 
landscapes within a 100-km radius of our production 
facilities around Pune and Sanand. These landscapes 
were studied using satellite image analysis, thematic 
overlays and on-ground ecological evaluation. This 
led to mapping of around 11,800 Wetlands across 15

religious importance, they are a keystone species

In Jharkhand, we are working to develop a pragmatic

which include ecological, human perception & focused

in collaboration with Lemsachenlok, a grassroots

we have planted 2.6 lakh saplings and protected across 
260 acres of community land. This community-led 
plantation on degraded Italics fallow lands, utilises 
indigenous knowledge of local communities to restore 
land cover with indigenous tree species. This NbS 
project will deliver restoration of degraded lands which 
builds ecological resilience and secures livelihoods 
of indigenous communities that rely on forests for 
sustenance and cultural practices.

Engagement of our technician workforce remains a key

participation, and digital empowerment.

technicians with seamless access to essential services

productivity. The platform also promotes continuous 
learning through bite-sized video modules, while digital 
notice boards ensure timely, transparent, and consistent 
communication across the shop floor. 
•	 Complementing this, technicians are actively engaged 
through structured forums, including Suggestion 
Schemes, Self-Directed and Self-Managed Teams, Kaizens, 
and Quality Circles, fostering a culture of ownership, 
problem-solving, and continuous improvement. 
•	 Regular town halls and joint councils further strengthen 
two-way communication, ensuring alignment, voice, 
and participation at every level. Together, these 
initiatives reinforce an inclusive and collaborative work 
environment, driving higher engagement, capability 
building, and operational excellence.
•	 Pragati programme: Our Pragati initiative enables 
technicians to pursue higher education through diploma 
programmes offered by reputed institutes located near 
our manufacturing plants. This voluntary programme has 
seen strong employee participation, reflecting a proactive 
intent to upskill and grow. Upon completion, participants 
are provided opportunities to transition into staff roles 
and further pursue BE/B.Tech programmes, supporting 
long-term career progression and capability building and 
talent pipeline for the organisation. Each of our sites has 
at least one ongoing Pragati batch.
Driving shopfloor excellence & engagement through 
Self-Directed Teams and Self-Managed Teams
•	 At TMPVL, we continue to nurture a culture of ownership, 
accountability, and empowerment on the shopfloor 
through the implementation of Self-Directed Teams 
(SDTs) and Self-Managed Teams (SMTs). These teams, 
independently run by technicians and contract workmen, 
are central to driving performance and fostering a 
participative work environment across our plants.
•	 Operating with a high degree of autonomy, SDTs and 
SMTs are empowered to take proactive ownership 
of critical pillars such as Safety, Quality, Productivity, 
Delivery, Cost, Morale, and Environment (SQPDCME) 
within their work areas. This structure enables team 
members to identify opportunities, solve problems at 
the source, and take swift action aligned with 
organisational goals.
•	 Beyond operational efficiency, this initiative significantly 
enhances engagement and collaboration with our 
business partners, reinforcing mutual respect, shared 
responsibility, and transparency.
•	 The culture of SDTs and SMTs ensures that the 
Company’s Balanced Scorecard (BSC), objectives, and 
communication are effectively cascaded to every 
individual on the ground. 
•	 This bottom-up approach is a cornerstone in our journey 
toward operational excellence, sustainable growth, and 
building a truly agile, empowered organisation.

Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA)
At TMPVL/TPEML risk assessment is done through Hazard 
Identification & Risk Assessment (HIRA) standard. HIRA 
standard guides the assessment methodology for each of the 
activities in the manufacturing operations.
Hazards at workplace are identified through HIRA for all 
routine activities/sub-activities. Cross functional team is 
formed to brainstorm & identify all hazards. All activities at 
TMPVL/TPEML are mapped and hazards are identified for 
each of these activities’ basis nature of activity, history of 
incidents and experience of workers. For all such identified 
hazards, risk is calculated based on Severity and Likelihood. 
Unit of measure of risk is Risk Priority Number (RPN).
Every hazard is categorised into Trivial, Tolerable, Moderate, 
Substantial and Intolerable. These hazards are then mitigated 
using hierarchy of controls. 
For non-routine activities risk assessment is done through Job 
safety analysis (JSA) which in itself is a separate standard.
The Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) process 
is tightly integrated into safety governance and operational 
decision making, with focused application in emerging 
and high risk domains such as EV battery handling. This 
integrated approach positions TMPVL/TPEML as future ready, 
risk resilient, and aligned with evolving technological and 
regulatory landscapes.

1 	Carbon net zero
Climate change remains one of the defining strategic 
challenges of our time. The automotive sector plays a pivotal 
role in global emissions and, therefore, holds significant 
influence in accelerating the transition to a low-carbon 
economy. As a manufacturer of luxury vehicles, we recognise 
our responsibility to lead this transformation. Therefore, 
responding to this challenge is not simply an environmental 
obligation, it is a business imperative. 
Our ambition is to achieve net zero by 2039 across our 
direct product emissions, operations and supply chain. This 
ambition aligns with a 1.5oC pathway and is underpinned 
by science-based targets that guide our decarbonisation 
pathway and ensure our actions align with the latest 
climate science. Our ambition reflects not only the scale of 
the challenge but the scale of the opportunity to redefine 
modern luxury through sustainability; strengthening our 
resilience, enhancing long-term competitiveness, and 
contributing meaningfully to a sustainable future.  
Reducing lifecycle emissions requires decisive action and 
continuous collaboration and innovation. Yet the speed 
of this transition will be shaped as much by consumer 
behaviour as by the efforts of manufacturers. An evolving 
regulatory environment and the ongoing development 
of charging infrastructure will be critical in influencing 
consumer confidence in electrification. 
These external factors introduce uncertainty that could 
significantly impact our ability to deliver against our mid-
term science-based targets. To strengthen governance and 
transparency, we are developing a Climate Transition Plan 
that will enable us to communicate these risks effectively, 
demonstrate a credible pathway to net zero, and embed the 
appropriate internal oversight needed to deliver it. 
The following sections reflect our performance in FY26 as 
well as our key initiatives across our operational and product 
emissions. The reported results are in alignment with the 
scope of our Reporting Methodology Statement available 
on our corporate website. Reported Scope 1 and 2 data, 
therefore, only includes those sites which are within the 
scope of our SBTi reporting requirements.
Operational emissions – 
Scope 1 and 2
Our operational emissions arise mainly from three sources: 
Scope 1 emissions produced by gas combustion for heat and 
power at our facilities and emissions from company-owned 
vehicles, and Scope 2 emissions associated with purchased 
electricity. Achieving net zero operational emissions will 
require us to cut energy use through greater efficiency, to 
transition to renewable electricity and to phase out gas 
consumption by electrifying our heat and energy systems. 
Performance
In FY26, our absolute Scope 1 and 2 emissions reduced to 
221.3 ktCO2e. This was an 11.3 per cent reduction compared 
to FY25 and a 32.1 per cent reduction compared to our 
location-based FY20 baseline, placing the results ahead of 
the required SBTi trajectory to be aligned to a 1.5oC pathway 
(25.2%). The result was affected by the cyber incident 
during which production was paused for five weeks before 
restarting on 8 October. However, the remaining months 
still achieved a 29.5 per cent reduction compared to the 
equivalent baseline months in FY20.
Key initiatives
The significant reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions in FY26 
was achieved through continued improvement in energy 
efficiency, particularly to heating and ventilation at key sites, 
as well as the installation of increased renewable energy 
capacity aligned with our strategic focus areas. 
1. Nitra, Slovakia, flue gas heat recovery 
The Nitra facility advanced its decarbonisation, roadmap 
through the installation, of a flue gas heat recovery system 
during summer 2025. This initiative captures and reuses 
waste heat from existing processes, reducing reliance on 
primary energy sources. The project represents a scalable 
model for energy efficiency improvements across the wider 
manufacturing network.

Supply chain and product  
emissions – Scope 3 
Our Scope 3 emissions are heavily influenced by the 
emissions produced when our vehicles are driven. 
Electrifying our portfolio is, therefore, fundamental to our 
science-based targets and realising our net zero ambition. A 
key milestone on this journey is our commitment for every 
brand to offer a pure-electric option by 2030, but progress 
toward these goals will rely on sustained consumer demand 
for battery electric vehicles. At the same time, we must 
avoid shifting emissions upstream into our supply chain by 
partnering with our suppliers to decarbonise key materials 
and expand the use of recycled content.

Our FY26 performance remained stable in comparison to the 
previous financial year but continued to deliver increased 
engagement and integration of the reductions achieved 
by our partners in the value chain. Our Scope 3 ‘use of 
sold product’ emissions for FY26 were 241.65 gCO2e per 
vehicle km. This was a reduction of 5.6 per cent compared 
to our FY20 baseline but a marginal increase of 1.2 per cent 
compared to our FY25 performance.

goods and services’ emissions for FY26 were 61.2 tCO2e/
vehicle. This was a 4.8 per cent reduction compared to our

this was partially offset by a slight increase the proportion 
of PHEVs retailed. The launch of the Range Rover Electric 
and subsequent BEV variants in the coming years should 
accelerate the reduction in our Scope 3 emissions towards 
2030 and beyond.

retail volume in comparison to previous years, our 
absolute Scope 3 emissions across these categories were 
21.6 MtCO2e, a reduction of 16.9 per cent compared to our 
FY25 performance.

In FY26, we continued to make progress, in collaboration 
with our supplier partners, to reduce emissions associated 
with our upstream value chains. The largest sources of

1. Sourcing
We have now firmly embedded CO2e targets for high-impact 
materials (>25kgCO2e) into the sourcing of new-tooled 
components, with more than 90 per cent of applicable 
projects achieving their CO2e targets in FY26. These targets 
are calculated by identifying best-in-class benchmarks 
across our supply base, which are continually assessed and 
revised to ensure progress towards net zero. We have also 
established a ‘Chain of Custody Standard’ which creates a 
consistent, transparent framework for tracking responsibly 
sourced, low-carbon materials through complex supply 
chains, improving traceability while ensuring environmental 
benefits are clearly and accurately accounted for.
Through this process, we have moved the majority of 
aluminium used on future products to low-carbon sources 
through the use of recycled material and virgin material 
from smelters using renewable electricity. We have also 
increased the use of recycled steel and polymers, and 
reduced the intensity of our glass components, as well as 
increased the use of low-carbon energy throughout our 
supply chain.
2. Procurement training and development
We have continued to develop and rollout training for our 
buyers to increase carbon literacy when engaging with 
suppliers on CO2e targets. This year, we launched a ‘CO2e 
Champions Network’, a group of buyers and procurement 
managers covering all areas of production spend, who 
receive additional training on decarbonisation and are 
increasingly taking on a lead role within ideation for 
supplier decarbonisation.

In FY26 we joined the launch of ‘Responsible Glass’, a global 
initiative that brings together organisations across the glass 
supply chain to develop a shared sustainability standard for

at a pivotal moment as it moves toward circular, low-carbon 
technologies. By contributing our decarbonisation expertise

value creation.

battery cell carbon intensity in line with our Reimagine 
strategy by maximising clean energy use and applying 
circular economy principles, both of which are key elements 
of Tata’s Project Aalingana. Together, this helps support a 
secure, competitive supply of battery cells while improving 
confidence in future raw material availability and responsible

resource efficiency
The resources we use and consume remain central to the 
environmental impact of our supply chain, operations, and 
products in use. Achieving our net zero ambition requires 
accelerating the transition to a circular economy, reducing 
our footprint while creating value and building a more 
resilient business model.
In FY26, we focused on making the resources we use more 
circular by implementing our key strategic objectives and 
progressing tracking systems deeper into our operations and 
product development. Our approach continues to be guided 
by three core circularity targets in relation to recycled 
content, waste and water:
•	 Increase recycled content by doubling and aiming to 
treble recycled content in new products from 2028
•	 Achieve zero waste to landfill and raise non-metallic 
waste recycling/reuse to 80 per cent by FY30
•	 Reduce water consumption by cutting water usage per 
vehicle produced by one-third by FY30 compared to 
FY20 levels
The following sections outline our progress in these areas 
during the past financial year.
1. Recycled content
We advanced our sustainable materials strategy by 
becoming the first automotive manufacturer to commit 
to introducing tyres made with more than 70 per cent 
renewable and recycled content across our luxury vehicle 
brands. Developed in partnership with Pirelli, the new P 
Zero tyres incorporate innovative materials such as silica 
derived from rice husks, plant-based resins, recycled carbon 
black, and recycled steel, all engineered to maintain high 
performance while significantly reducing environmental 
impact. The tyres will initially be fitted on select Range 
Rover models then across our wider portfolio, supporting 
our broader ambitions for responsible sourcing and lower-
carbon product design. This initiative sits adjacent to our 
recycled-content target by accelerating the adoption of 
sustainable, circular materials within the supply chain.
We progressed our closed-loop recycling of polyurethane 
seat foam, developed with Dow’s MobilityScience™ and 
Adient. Early trials demonstrated that end-of-life foam can 
be successfully recycled into high-quality polyols suitable 
for manufacturing new seat cushions, helping to reduce 
dependence on virgin materials. The technology is now 
advancing to production scale testing, marking an important 
step toward circular interior materials.
To support our aim to increase recycled content in our new 
vehicles from 2028, we are expanding the use of recycled 
aluminium sheet.
2. Zero waste to landfill
We strengthened waste segregation practices across 
sites to support our zero-landfill ambition. These actions 
lay the foundation for a more resource-efficient future. 
Underpinning this is the reuse of clay used for modelling 
which upon reaching the end of its useful life can be

the cars of today – symbolic of how the same material that 
defined the past is helping create the future. This approach 
helps to ensure a more circular approach, aligning with 
our Reimagine strategy to deliver modern luxury in a more 
sustainable way.

3 	Nature and biodiversity
In February 2025, governments concluded biodiversity 
finance and monitoring negotiations at the resumed UN 
Biodiversity Conference (CBD COP16). While not directly 
binding on companies, these outcomes shape the policy and 
investor context for businesses with global operations and 
supply chains.1
Policy and market attention is increasingly focused on 
nature-based solutions as part of the response to climate 
change and biodiversity loss. External studies indicate that 
nature-based solutions could contribute around 30 per cent 
of the global emissions reductions required to meet Net 
Zero pathways, while also delivering benefits for ecosystem 
resilience and communities.2
Strategy
During the reporting period, we undertook an assessment of 
the nature-related impacts, risks and opportunities across 
our direct freehold site operations and upstream supply 
chain. The activity focused on understanding how our 
operations and value chain interact with nature, identifying 
areas of higher potential impact or risk, and ways to embed 
these considerations into existing corporate processes and 
decision-making.
The assessment covered ten freehold sites, seven in the UK 
and three internationally, alongside an initial screening of 
upstream supply chain activities. This provided a consistent 
view of where our direct operations and key supply chain 
stages interact most with nature across our global footprint. 
The assessment highlighted that nature-related impacts, 
risks and opportunities arise from both direct operational 
activities and upstream supply chains. Key themes relate to 
how land, resources and emissions are managed across the 
value chain with differing levels of visibility and influence 
between site operations and upstream activities.
This work has informed the development of a Biodiversity 
Roadmap, which sets out targeted actions to manage 
nature-related impacts and risks and to deliver improvements 
over time. Rather than creating parallel systems, the Roadmap 
focuses on practical delivery, alignment with existing plans 
and processes, and integration into business decision-making.
This work is aligned with recognised global and group-
level frameworks, including the Kunming-Montreal Global 
Biodiversity Framework and the Tata Group Biodiversity 
Management Framework. It also supports compliance 
with evolving regulatory requirements, including the 
EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, by 
strengthening how nature-related impacts, risks and 
opportunities are identified and addressed within existing 
governance and reporting processes.3

Sustainable supply chain
Our sustainability journey continues to be shaped by a  
vision that looks beyond mobility—towards creating a 
cleaner and healthier world for generations to come.  
With a long‑term ambition to achieve net‑zero emissions 
by 2040, we recognise that progress of this scale depends 
on shared responsibility and collective action. This is why 
we work closely with our suppliers to embed responsible 
practices across the value chain. What began as a 
conventional supply network has steadily evolved into a 
partnership of purpose, grounded in trust, respect, and 
collaboration. The concluded financial year reaffirmed this 
belief: lasting transformation happens when every partner 
moves forward together, united by common goals and 
supported by clear pathways. Building on this collective 
commitment, our sustainability efforts are organised 
through a structured framework that ensures alignment, 
accountability, and purposeful progress across our 
supply chain.
Tata Motor’s sustainable supply 
chain framework 
Our Sustainable Supply Chain Framework is designed 
to integrate sustainability into everyday decisions and 
long‑term choices across the value chain. The framework is 
structured around four guiding pillars—Ambition, Policies, 
Process, and Enablers—each strengthened through strategic 
decisions, collective actions, and seamless execution during 
FY26. The implementation and oversight of supply chain 
sustainability programmes are overseen by the Executive 
Management, who report regularly to the Board of Directors 
on performance and strategic direction.
1   Ambition
Our ambition defines the direction of responsible growth 
across the supply chain. It aligns supplier partners with Tata 
Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited’s broader sustainability 
priorities and sets clear expectations for collective progress. 
This ambition is translated into clear KPIs and targets, 
creating a strong foundation for meaningful and measurable 
progress. These targets are communicated through 
structured engagements, Aikyam forums, and supplier 
conferences, ensuring suppliers have clarity on expectations 
and the pathway ahead.
By anchoring ambition in measurable supplier‑level 
indicators, we foster transparency, shared accountability, 
and continuous improvement across the ecosystem. With 
direction established, effective governance ensures this 
intent is consistently reflected in everyday actions, strategic 
decisions, and long‑term development of our supplier base.
2   Policies — Governance with integrity and purpose
Our Value Chain Partner Code of Conduct and 
procurement policies articulate clear expectations on 
ethics, environmental performance, human rights, safety, 
and business integrity—providing a common foundation 
for all supplier engagements. These frameworks are 
periodically reviewed and strengthened to reflect regulatory 
developments, emerging sustainability priorities, and 
evolving business needs.
Regular engagements help suppliers understand both the 
requirements and the intent behind them, reinforcing a 
culture anchored in fairness, transparency, and responsible 
conduct. Policies are deployed through structured processes 
supported by key enablers, ensuring that expectations are 
consistently translated into action across the organisation. 
3   Process — Building resilience with 
robust processes
Sustainability is woven into every stage of supplier 
engagement. This includes manufacturing site assessments, 
structured onboarding, and an annual ESG Supplier 
Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ). These assessments 
help identify strengths, understand gaps, and guide 
improvement plans where required. Risk‑management 
frameworks are being strengthened to proactively identify 
and mitigate risks, supporting seamless governance and 
continuous improvement.
Strengthening this foundation, in FY26, we introduced 
Prakriti, a digital ESG data management platform launched 
at the Annual Supplier Conference. Prakriti moves us from 
manual assessments to a unified, analytics‑driven system 
aligned with widely recognised ESG frameworks. Suppliers 
and internal teams were trained prior to rollout, ensuring

At the core of our enablement strategy is Aikyam—a Sanskrit

strengthening capabilities across the ecosystem.

support suppliers and ecosystem partners with hands‑on 
guidance as they progress through their sustainability 
journeys, helping build capacity and strengthen ESG

BUSINESS PERFORMANCE
The Indian Passenger Vehicle (‘PV’) industry saw its 
highest-ever volumes in FY26 of over 4.6 million units, on the 
back of GST 2.0, which enhanced vehicle affordability and 
drove a sharp increase in customer demand. The segmental 
shifts in the industry continued to gain momentum with strong 
double-digit growth across SUVs, CNG vehicles and EVs.
In FY26, the PV business (including Electric Vehicles), achieved 
its highest-ever sales of 6,41,586 units, including a record 
10,201 units of sales in international market. The PV business 
outpaced the industry, growing at 15% compared to FY25, on 
the back of strong growth in second half of FY26, where it 
emerged as the #2 ranked manufacturer in the industry. The 
launch of the new nameplate Tata Sierra, New Tata Punch, 
New Tata Altroz and petrol versions of Harrier and Safari have 
been well received in the market.
Tata Passenger Electric Mobility Limited 
(‘TPEML’)
The Indian Electric Vehicle (‘EV’) industry experienced 
significant growth in FY26, recording an increase of over 
80% compared to the previous year. This growth was driven 
by increased participation from manufacturers, multiple 
launches across the industry and growing positive customer 
sentiment towards EVs.
In FY26, the EV business sustained its market leadership 
position, commanding over 40% market share of the 
EV Industry with highest-ever sales of 92,179 units. The 
business saw strong growth on the back of the launches of 
Harrier.ev and new Punch.ev, both of which received positive 
customer traction. The business took key efforts to drive EV 
mainstreaming by addressing barriers to adoption through 
higher range products, provision of lifetime battery warranty, 
price parity with conventional powertrains and expansion of 
charging infrastructure through focused efforts.
Please refer to the paragraph on Passenger Vehicles and 
Electric Vehicles in the Management Discussion & Analysis 
section for detailed analysis.
Jaguar Land Rover (‘JLR’)
JLR (as per IFRS) recorded revenue of £22.9 billion in FY26, 
as compared to £29.0 billion in FY25. The decline in revenue 
was primarily attributable to lower wholesales (excluding 
the China joint venture), which decreased to 3,07,915 units, 
along with an 18% decline in retail sales to 3,52,389 units. 
Profitability was also impacted, with the underlying EBITDA 
margin at 6.7%, reflecting lower wholesales and retails. Profit 
before tax and exceptional items stood at £14 million in FY26, 
as against £2.5 billion in FY25. A loss after tax of £244 million 
was reported, compared to a profit of £1.8 billion in the 
previous year.

FINANCE & CREDIT RATING
During FY26, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Group (‘the 
Group’) generated negative free cashflows, largely due to 
impact on volumes from production stoppages and working 
capital movements following cyber incident at Jaguar Land 
Rover (‘JLR’).
The Consolidated Net Debt stood at ₹30,710 crore at the end 
of FY26 as compared to a Net Cash position ₹1,018 crore at the 
end of FY25. The Group significantly shored up the liquidity 
post JLR cyber incident and continues to maintain sufficient 
liquidity to navigate the impact of external challenges. As at 
March 31, 2026, the Group liquidity for domestic operations 
was ₹9,601 crore, whereas the liquidity at JLR was £6.9 billion 
(including unutilized credit facility of £4.2 billion).
In June 2025, Moodys upgraded JLR’s long term issuer credit 
rating from Ba2/Positive to Ba1/Positive incorporating a 
one-notch parental support uplift.
Post the cyber incident at JLR, Moody’s and S&P changed 
the outlook on JLR long term issuer credit rating to Negative. 
As a result, JLR’s long term issuer credit rating assigned by 
Moody’s and S&P stood at Ba1/Negative and BBB-/Negative, 
respectively. As a result of this development, the outlook on 
the Company’s long term issuer credit rating was changed to 
Negative and the credit rating assigned by Moody’s and S&P 
stood at Ba1/Negative and BBB/Negative, respectively.
The Company’s long-term credit rating assigned by CRISIL, 
ICRA and CARE remained unchanged at AA+/Stable.
Please refer to the paragraph on Credit Ratings in Corporate 
Governance Report and Liquidity and Capital Resources 
in the Management Discussion & Analysis section for 
detailed analysis.

SAFETY & HEALTH – PERFORMANCE & 
INITIATIVES
SAFETY
At the Company safety is not merely a compliance protocol, it is 
a core value and non-negotiable commitment that underpins 
the operations. The Company’s Safety Management System 
is aligned & guided by ISO 45001:2018, Integrated Safety 
Management System, the Company continue to cultivate a 
Zero Harm Culture that protects lives, fosters well-being and 
prepares the Company for the future of mobility.
Occupational Safety is governed through a comprehensive 
multi-tiered structure led by the Safety, Health & Sustainability 
(‘SHS’) Board & SHS Committee, supported by SHS Councils, 
Corporate Sub-Committees and Plant Apex Committees for 
seamless strategic-to-operational integration.
In FY26, the safety agenda was anchored through four 
strategic focus areas:
•	
Leadership 
Behaviour 
and 
Safety 
Governance: 
Throughout the year, the Company further strengthened 
the Safety Culture Model through sustained leadership 
engagement and structured communication across 
all levels of the organisation. Eight critical leadership 
behaviours were systematically embedded through 
dedicated 
leadership 
forums, 
capability-building 
interventions and governance platforms. This effort 
was supported by the simplification and revision of core 
Safety Standards, developed with expert input from 
dss+. The updated standards address emerging 
and evolving risk areas, including Electric Vehicles, 
Hydrogen, LNG and Renewable Energy systems. These 
standards have been rolled out across all plants and are 
actively monitored to ensure effective implementation, 
compliance and long-term sustainability. In parallel, 
several 
focused 
leadership-led 
safety 
programs 
were implemented, including the Leadership Model 
& Cascade, Leader as Trainer, Leader as Mentor 
initiatives. Operational risk reduction measures such 
as micro-zone realignment at shops and plant roads, 
forklift traffic reduction and strengthened pedestrian 
safety interventions were also underway & deployed, 
reinforcing visible leadership, ownership and on-ground 
risk mitigation.
•	
Business Partner Safety Management: The Company’s 
Business Partner Safety Program, structured around 
six key levers and a risk-based partner categorization 
framework, has been implemented across all vendor 
categories. During the year, Star Rating assessments 
were carried in each of the quarter for high-risk job 
performing business partner, enabling systematic 
performance evaluation and targeted improvement 
actions. In addition, 59 Self-Managed Teams (SMTs) were 
established across plants, supported by a well-defined 
roadmap for progressive capability development. 
Aligned with the Company’s commitment to dignity 
and inclusion, focused initiatives were undertaken 
during the year to enhance driver dignity and improve 
amenities for conservancy staff, thereby reinforcing 
a respectful, inclusive and safe working environment 
across the extended value chain.
•	
Digital & AI for Safety: The Company’s digital safety 
transformation is guided by strategic themes such as 
leveraging digital technologies in LOTO, Video Analytics, 
Connected Assets, Safety Management Systems. During 
the year, the Company developed AI models to enable 
predictive and preventive safety interventions and 
deployed 1,911 digital and technological safety controls 
across all plants, strengthening risk anticipation, real-
time monitoring and proactive incident prevention.
•	
Reward and Recognition Culture: The Company promote 
a strong culture of safety through a structured Reward 
and Recognition framework that acknowledges and 
celebrates safety champions across the Company and 
the Business Partners. This includes on the Spot Awards, 
Best Self-Managed Team (SMT) recognitions, Safety 
Point Leaders and Safety Stewards. These initiatives are 
complemented by plant-level Safety Competitions and 
quarterly Business Partner Reward Programs, which 
collectively incentivise proactive safety behaviour, 
reinforce accountability and embed safety excellence 
across the organisation and its extended value chain.
While the Company continue to maintain a vigilant safety 
approach, but overall LTIFR has increased by 7.6% in FY26 
whereas at workplace it has gone down by 7.6%. We 
are addressing the underlying root causes and targeted 
recommendations are being rolled out across all plants to 
arrest and reverse this trend.
Looking ahead, the Company remain committed to embedding 
safety into every process and decision by leveraging digital 
intelligence, fostering inclusive partnerships with business 
partners and building a resilient Zero Harm workplace 
driven by the Company’s safety culture model and eight 
leadership behaviours.

ENERGY & ENVIRONMENT
The Company has always been conscious of the need to 
conserve energy in its manufacturing plants and to protect 
the environment. Energy conservation is achieved through 
optimized consumption of power and fossil fuels and through 
improvements in energy productivity via Energy Conservation 
(‘ENCON’) projects. These efforts contribute to reducing 
operational costs and mitigating climate change by lowering 
greenhouse gas emissions.
The Company is also a signatory to RE100, a collaborative, 
global initiative of influential businesses committed to 100% 
renewable electricity. It is actively working towards increasing 
the amount of renewable energy generated in-house and 
procured from off-site sources.
In FY26, ENCON efforts contributed to energy savings of 
28.53 lakh kWh of electricity, resulting in the avoidance 
of 2025 tonnes of CO₂ emissions. During the same year, 
the Company generated or sourced 179.8 million kWh of 
renewable electricity for its manufacturing operations, 
representing 83% of the total power consumption for its 
Passenger Vehicle operations, and thereby avoiding 1.27 lakh 
tonnes of CO₂ emissions.
The Company generates renewable energy (RE) in-house 
through solar photovoltaic (PV) installations and off-site 
captive wind farms. Additionally, it procures off-site wind and 
solar power through “Power Purchase Agreements” (PPAs) 
and International Renewable Energy Certificates (i-RECs). As 
of March 31, 2026, the Company’s in-house installed Solar 
PV capacity are Chikhali, Pune (TMPV): 18.9 MWp, Sanand, 
Gujarat (TMPV): 2 MWp and Sanand, Gujarat (TPEM): 
0.4 MWp.
In FY26, the Company also reduced fresh water withdrawal 
through effluent recycling and rainwater harvesting. The 
plants at Sanand (TMPV), have achieved Water Neutral 
certification as per CII-GBC standards. The remaining plants 
are working towards achieving similar certifications.
Furthermore, in FY26, the Company sustained its efforts 
across all plants to divert hazardous waste from landfill or 
incineration and to derive value from such waste. Several 
plants divert hazardous waste for energy recovery through 
co-processing at cement plants. All three plants, i.e., Chikhali, 
Sanand (TMPV), Sanand (TPEM) have achieved Zero Waste to 
Landfill certification as per CII-GBC standards.

1.	 Overview:
	
	
At Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited 
(Formerly Tata Motors Limited) (hereinafter 
referred to as TMPVL or the Company), Corporate 
Social Responsibility (‘CSR’) is an integral part of 
our commitment to being a responsible corporate 
citizen. We are dedicated to enhancing the quality 
of life in the communities we serve. The Company’s 
CSR initiatives are rooted in the values of nation-
building, 
sustainable 
development, 
inclusive 
growth, and social equity.
	
	
As part of the Tata Group, a global institution 
that not only excels in business but also upholds 
community well-being as a core purpose, we 
are committed to strategically integrating our 
social responsibilities with our pursuit of business 
excellence. In doing so, we aim to create long-term 
value for all our stakeholders.
	
	
The Company remains responsive to the needs of 
its key stakeholders, particularly the socially and 
economically disadvantaged. The Company’s CSR 
focus includes the underprivileged, marginalized, 
vulnerable communities and especially those 
considered under the Tata Group’s Affirmative 
Action agenda, such as, the Scheduled Castes, 
the Scheduled Tribes, Persons with Disabilities, 
Women, and other disadvantaged groups. (Tata 
Affirmative Action Program (TAAP) is focused on 
reducing inequalities faced by socially backward 
groups (Ref. Sr. No. iii of Schedule VII of the 
Companies Act, 2013 (‘the Act’)).
	
	
In line with the Tata Group’s CSR agenda, our 
initiatives and efforts are aligned with national and 
international developmental priorities, including 
the Sustainable Development Goals (‘SDGs’), and 
confirm to Schedule VII of the Act, and are guided 
by the CSR Committee and approved by the Board 
of Directors.
	
	
To 
maximize 
impact 
and 
leverage 
India’s 
demographic dividend, our CSR priorities include:
	
	
•	
Health and Well-being
	
	
•	
Education and Skill Development
	
	
•	
Employability and Livelihoods
	
	
•	
Conservation of Environment, Biodiversity 
and Nature
	
	
•	
Rural Development, with emphasis on 
water restoration and Integrated Village 
Development Programs (‘IVDP’), and
	
	
•	
Preservation of Nature and Biodiversity.
	
	
The Company’s interventions primarily target 
regions in and around our business footprint and 
also extend support to underserved geographies 
and aspirational districts across India.
	
	
The Company’s CSR is anchored in the philosophy 
of ‘More from Less for More’, emphasizing the 
efficient use of financial and human resources 
to create greater impact through strategic 
partnerships and collaborative efforts.
	
	
The Company was committed to fostering a strong 
culture of employee volunteering and leveraging 
our core competencies - managerial, technological, 
and operational - to innovate and scale our CSR 
programs, with the goal of delivering measurable, 
lasting impact and contributing meaningfully to the 
communities we serve.

under five core thrust areas, along with a focused 
Rural Development programme especially the 
Integrated Village Development Initiative (IVDP).

Focus on child malnutrition, preventive 
and curative healthcare, health awareness

exam preparation support, co-curricular 
activities, school infrastructure development,

A.	 CONSERVATION OF ENERGY
	
The Company has always been conscious of the need 
to conserve energy in its Manufacturing Plants which 
leads to optimized consumption of non-renewable fossil 
fuels, energy productivity, climate change mitigation, 
and reduction in operational costs. The Company is also 
signatory to RE100 - a collaborative, global initiative of 
influential businesses committed to 100% renewable 
electricity, and is working to increase the amount of 
renewable energy generated in-house and procured 
from off-site sources. 
	
(i)	 The 
steps 
taken 
or 
impact 
on 
conservation of energy:
	
	
Energy Conservation (‘ENCON’) projects have been 
implemented at across Plants of the Company in a 
planned and budgeted manner. Some of the major 
ENCON projects in FY26 include:
	
	
•	
Electrical 
Energy 
Savings 
through 
LED 
Installation 
by 
Replacing 
Conventional 
Lighting Systems in Sanand, TPEM.
	
	
•	
Electrical Energy Savings via Heat Exchange 
Optimization of Chiller in Sanand, TPEM.
	
	
•	
Compressed 
air 
retention 
initiatives 
implemented across shops, including a 
compressed air leakage arresting drive and 
shutdown of compressed air supply during 
B & C shifts, block closure days, and non-
production days in Sanand, TMPV.
	
	
•	
Optimization of both shower tester operations 
through VFD implementation for rainwater 
usage Sanand, TMPV.
	
	
These ENCON efforts in FY26 have resulted into 
energy savings of 28.53 lakh kWh electricity, 
resulting   into   avoided   emission   of   2025 tCO2.
	
(ii) 	The steps taken by the Company for 
utilizing alternate sources of energy:
	
	
The Company continued to add on-site Renewable 
Energy (solar) generation capacity in FY 2026, which 
brings the total installed capacity to 21.3 MWp:
	
	
•	
Chikhali, Pune (TMPV): 18.9 MWp
	
	
•	
Sanand, Gujarat (TMPV): 2 MWp
	
	
•	
Sanand, Gujarat (TPEM): 0.4 MWp
	
	
The Company also sources off-site renewable 
energy through Power Purchase Agreements (PPA) 
with Third Party Wind & Solar Power Generators 
and Green Energy Purchase from Exchange & 
Discom and I-REC’s (international renewable 
energy certificates). The Company plans to 
continue to source off-site renewable power in line 
with regulatory policies / frameworks and tariffs 
in the States where we operate. These efforts will 
continue to help offset greenhouse gas emissions 
in the coming years. 
	
	
In FY26, the Company generated / sourced 179.8 
million kWh of renewable electricity for its 
manufacturing operations, which amounts to 83% 
of the total power consumption for the Passenger 
Vehicle operations. This contributed to avoidance 
1.27 lakh tonnes of CO₂ .
	
(iii)	 The 
capital 
investment 
on 
energy 
conservation equipment:
	
	
In FY26, the Company had invested ₹38.47 lakhs in 
various energy conservation projects.

equitable world for all. The Company's commitment to these principles has positioned it as not only a leader in 
the automotive sector but also a champion of social equity and inclusivity. 
	
	
	
The Company respects differences that are fundamental to an individual’s identity, such as age, gender, ethnicity, 
race, physical ability, mental ability, and sexual orientation, as well as latent and invisible differences that shape 
our perspectives, like education, work experience, parental status, etc. The Company is committed to being an 
equal opportunity employer, maintaining dignity and respect for all.

moving beyond gender and have received well-accepted dipstick research to support this as well.

health and safety, labor rights, and human rights. By setting these standards, the Company aims to foster responsible 
business practices among our suppliers and partners. Manufacturing Site Audit questionnaire is updated to include a

for its suppliers through the Digital portal “Prakriti”.  Today, Prakriti enables structured ESG data collection across Tier I

as specified by the operating permits, consents, and authorizations. It received a large and diverse number of parts, 
components, and consumables in various forms of packaging which are discarded. These are segregated as per material 
type and shape and sold to re-cyclers for conversion and utilization. This ensures the sale of all flexible and rigid plastic 
packaging to authorized plastic waste processors for re-cycling and utilization in manufacture of new packaging material.
